slides.title: Evaluating agent skills
slides.text: Eleven ways to find out whether a SKILL.md file actually helps, and the method behind each one.
slides.notes: Welcome. This deck covers the ideas only. The Python files in the course show the code.

slides.title: A skill is instructions loaded on demand

cards.title: What that means
lines: A folder with a SKILL.md: a name, a description, and a procedure
The harness (Claude Code and friends) reads the description to decide when to load it
The model never sees the body until the skill is loaded

cards.title: Why it needs evals
lines: A skill that never loads fails silently: no error, no log line
A skill that loads can still be ignored, half-followed, or overridden
Most software engineering skills measured so far add little or nothing

slides.notes: Two failure modes to keep in mind for the whole deck: not loading, and loading but not helping.

slides.title: Three groups, eleven eval types
slides.footer: Run them in this order. The free ones catch the cheap mistakes before you spend a single agent run.
slides.notes: Cost rises left to right. The third group re-reads what the second group saved, so it costs nothing.

slides.title: Structural lint
slides.question: Is this SKILL.md well-formed enough for a harness to load it at all?
method: Parse the frontmatter and check the spec: name format, name matches the folder, description length
Look for a trigger phrase in the description ("use when ...")
Check the body: unclosed code fences, referenced files that do not exist
watch: A name that does not match its folder never loads, and nothing tells you
Lint proves the file is loadable, not that it is good
slides.notes: Runs in milliseconds. Belongs in CI on every commit.

slides.title: Security scan
slides.question: Does the skill ask the agent to do something hostile?
method: Match every file against known-bad patterns: instruction overrides, hidden text, credential paths, data sent to remote hosts, piped installs
Score by severity, with repeat hits on the same rule counting less each time
Verdict bands: safe, review first, do not install
watch: Static scans have false positives; a skill about SSH will mention ~/.ssh
Never run the skill to test it. Read it.
slides.notes: A malicious skill is a prompt injection with a README. The agent obeys it because it looks like configuration.

slides.title: Offline routing
slides.question: Does the description use the words users type, without colliding with neighbouring skills?
method: Put every installed skill's description in a catalog
Rank the catalog against sample prompts with plain text similarity
Positives must rank your skill first; negatives must rank the rightful owner above it; no two descriptions may be near-duplicates
watch: This is not how the real harness routes, so a pass here is not proof of triggering
When a positive fails, fix the description, not the prompt
slides.notes: Free and deterministic. It caught a real vocabulary gap in the course's sample skill.

slides.title: Trigger eval
slides.question: Does the real harness load the skill when it should, and only then?
method: Write prompts that should trigger and prompts that should not; never name the skill
Run each prompt several times through the harness and watch for the skill being loaded
Count a prompt as triggered when at least half its runs fire; report precision and recall
watch: Testing only positives rewards a description that hijacks everything
Triggering is random; one run per prompt tells you nothing
slides.notes: The name and description are the whole triggering mechanism. Re-run this after every edit to them.

slides.title: Deterministic grading
slides.question: Does the output follow the rules we can check with code?
method: Turn every checkable rule into a function: regex for the format, a length limit, a required line
Prove the grader first: a hand-written perfect answer must pass, a wrong one must fail
Report pass rate per rule, not one blended score
watch: A grader that rejects the oracle measures the grader, not the skill
Rules a regex cannot express go to the judge, not into a looser regex
slides.notes: Code graders are cheap, reproducible, and tell you exactly which rule broke.

slides.title: Paired A/B comparison
slides.question: How much better is the agent with the skill than without it?
method: Same prompt, same model, same tools, same fresh workspace; the only difference is whether the skill files exist
Pair each with-skill run with a without-skill run of the same case
Report the difference in pass rate, the skill lift, never the absolute
watch: A flag that hides the skill is not enough; the files must be absent or the agent can read them
With skill 100 percent means nothing if the baseline was already 95
slides.notes: This is the eval everyone means by "does the skill work". Everything else supports it.

slides.title: LLM-as-judge
slides.question: What about the rules only a reader can check?
method: Rubric grader: one output, a list of binary assertions, pass or fail with quoted evidence
Pairwise comparator: two outputs labelled A and B, judged in both orders, blind to which had the skill
Structured output only; a score parsed out of prose is a bug waiting to happen
watch: Use a different model from the one under test
Feed the judge an empty reply and "I don't know" first; both must fail
Read the failures: the course's judge counted a code fence as commentary until someone looked
slides.notes: Treat the judge as an instrument that needs calibration, not as ground truth.

slides.title: Trajectory eval
slides.question: Did the agent follow the procedure and respect the prohibitions?
method: Record every tool call the agent makes, in order
Compliance: required steps happened, and in the right order (skill loaded before the work started)
Boundary: forbidden actions never happened, even when the user asked for them
watch: A perfect output can come from a skipped procedure; only the tool log shows it
The course's sample skill lost this one: asked directly, the agent ran git commit anyway
slides.notes: Score is trigger times the share of procedure steps followed, and any broken prohibition sets it to zero. No trigger, no score.

slides.title: Statistics over repeated runs
slides.question: Is the lift real, or noise?
method: pass@k: how often at least one of k attempts passes; pass^k: how often all k do
Bootstrap the paired differences to get an interval; if it straddles zero, you have not shown anything
A permutation test on the signs of the differences gives a p-value with no distribution assumptions
watch: Eight pairs cannot resolve a twenty-point effect; the noise floor is roughly one over the square root of the pair count
One run is an anecdote
slides.notes: A finding that looks solid on one run is often refuted by the fifth.

slides.title: Regression check
slides.question: Did anything get worse since the last run you trusted?
method: Save a baseline: the key metrics plus a hash of the skill's files
On every later run compare each metric against the baseline with a tolerance
A drop after the skill changed is expected churn; a drop with no change is drift in the model or harness
watch: Without the content hash you cannot tell your edit from the world moving under you
Skills rot; a check nobody runs catches nothing
slides.notes: Cheap to run because it reads saved results. The expensive part is refreshing them.

slides.title: Efficiency
slides.question: What does the improvement cost in tokens, money and time?
method: Take token counts from the API's usage data, including cached input; never estimate from text length
Compare quality delta against cost delta per arm
Classify: better and cheaper, a trade-off, cheaper but weaker, worse on both, or reject
watch: Loading a skill costs extra turns, and every turn reads the whole context again
Cost per passing run is the fair comparison between two skills
slides.notes: Quality up and cost up is a decision, not a verdict. Say the numbers and let the owner choose.

slides.eyebrow: What every good eval setup agrees on
slides.title: Six rules that matter more than any one eval
rules: Test the description before the body. A skill that does not load cannot help.
Grade with code where you can, and prove the grader on a known-good and a known-bad answer.
Pair the with and without runs, hold everything else fixed, report the delta with an interval.
Grade the end state and the tool log, not the transcript's narration.
Keep the skill files physically absent from the baseline workspace.
Save every raw row. Analysis should never need a new run.
slides.notes: If the audience remembers nothing else, these six.

slides.title: Three free checks, then one trigger eval, then one A/B
slides.text: Start with three test cases. If the skill helps on three, add five more. Twenty to fifty for CI. A hundred or more before you publish a number.
slides.notes: Small first. The eval that runs is worth more than the perfect eval that does not exist yet.
